draft.title: Discrimination and harassment at work
card: Discrimination
treating a worker or job applicant unfairly because of a personal attribute, such as sex, race, age or disability. Other attributes include pregnancy and marital status.
Sexual harassment
unwelcome sexual behaviour that a reasonable person would expect to offend, humiliate or intimidate. It does not matter whether the person meant harm.
Where the law comes from
Federal laws, such as the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) and the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth), apply to workplaces. The Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) also covers NSW workplaces.
Employer duty
An employer can be held responsible for the conduct of staff at work. Taking reasonable steps to prevent it, such as training and a complaints process, matters.
draft.remember: Workers must not be treated unfairly for who they are, and unwelcome sexual behaviour at work is unlawful.

a.q: Which situation is an example of unlawful discrimination at work?
opts: A firm refuses to hire a woman because she is pregnant
A firm refuses to hire a person with no relevant skills
A firm hires the applicant who interviewed best
A firm pays a worker more because of longer experience
a.why: Pregnancy is a protected attribute, so refusing to hire for that reason is unfair treatment. The option about no relevant skills is tempting, but it rests on ability, not a personal attribute.
a.clue: Look for a decision based on a personal attribute, not on skills or merit.

b.q: Dev's manager keeps making sexual jokes at him after Dev asks him to stop. The manager says he meant it as a laugh. Why can this still be sexual harassment?
opts: The jokes are unwelcome and a reasonable person would be offended
The manager has a higher position than Dev at the workplace
The jokes were repeated more than once during the same week
The manager meant to cause harm to Dev with the jokes
b.why: Sexual harassment depends on the behaviour being unwelcome and on what a reasonable person would expect, not on what the person meant. Intent is the tempting wrong answer because the manager claims it was a joke, but the card says it does not matter.
b.clue: Does the law ask what the harasser meant, or how a reasonable person would see it?
